11237-the-pearl-box-containing-one-hundr:
Compiled by a pastor for young readers, the Pearl Box promises one hundred moral stories, though a transcriber's note warns the volume holds fewer than that. Each short tale teaches a lesson about duty in private, social, and public life, from a dying boy's last wishes to everyday acts of kindness and obedience. The preface states the aim plainly: to make children wiser, happier, and more useful.

The stories are simple and sentimental by modern standards, and deliberately so. They belong to a nineteenth-century tradition of Sunday-school reading, where fiction served instruction first. For historians of childhood or religion, the book shows what adults thought children ought to learn from print.
11595-the-pearl-box-containing-one-hundr:
A pastor wrote this 1851 volume of one hundred beautiful stories for young people, aiming to teach duties by familiar tales. Each story carries a moral, and each teaches principles by which youth should be governed.

One tale follows Willy, whose mother, a Christian, tells her children that God is father to the fatherless and urges honesty, virtue, and faith. Another story in the set, glimpsed in the middle pages, turns on a guide for a child and a father in heaven who never leaves his own. The book is Sunday-school reading of its period, plain and earnest.
14762-now-or-never-or-the-adventures-of-:
Oliver Optic's 1872 story for young folks follows Bobby Bright, a smart boy whose struggles matter inside as well as outside. Its preface warns that worldly prosperity is not the truest victory, and that the hero's devotion to principles should carry the interest more than his success in business.

Bobby meets temptations on the plain of life, learns to master them, and gathers wealth and honours only as a second reward. Optic, author of The Boat Club and All Aboard, writes for boys who need models of pluck and honesty. The book is earnest, brisk and moral, in the style that made Optic a favourite schoolroom author of his day.
19026-the-boss-of-the-lazy-y:
Charles Alden Seltzer published this western novel in 1915, illustrated by J. Allen St. John. Its hero, Calumet Marston, comes home to the Lazy Y ranch and meets Betty, his guardian, and the duties of an heir. Calumet plays Betty's game, learns his first lessons, and faces a page from the past, a Toltec idol, and questions of responsibility.

Later chapters bring suspicion, jealousy, an ambush, a meeting in the Red Dog, and a tragedy in a timber grove, before Neal Taggart visits and tribal altars close the tale. Seltzer builds the plot on ranch management as much as on gunplay. Readers get a western about growing into authority, with romance, rivalry, and a hero who must earn his ranch.
24660-hope-and-have-or-fanny-grant-among:
Oliver Optic wrote this story for young people, published at Boston in 1866, under the motto from St. Paul: for we are saved by hope. Its heroine is Fanny Grant, who finds herself among the Indians, and its frontispiece shows the capture of an Indian boy. The tale follows Fanny's trials and courage in a frontier world.

Optic, author of the Army and Navy stories and the Boat Club, wrote for boys and girls who liked adventure with a moral. His heroine learns patience, faith, and kindness through danger. Young readers get a stirring, old-fashioned tale of a girl among the Indians, in the style of Optic's best work.
28131-the-nursery-march-1877-vol-xxi-no-:
The Nursery for March 1877, volume twenty-one, number three, continues the Boston monthly for youngest readers under John L. Shorey. Its prose leads with An Old-Time Scene, in which children rush to a playroom fireplace, and includes dancing lessons, astronomy, a rat hunt, and a woodchuck hunt. A drawing lesson and country tales round out the number.

Verse offers Tom-Tit, a Lenten song, a cat's mew, and a beach song, with one piece set to music by Linda Cantoni. The short items, pictures, and simple morals suit children just learning to read. The issue captures a quiet, home-centred world of pets, lessons, and outdoor play.
28132-the-nursery-april-1877-vol-xxi-no-:
The Nursery for April 1877, volume twenty-one, number four, is a Boston monthly for youngest readers. Its lead question, Why Did Elfrida Go to Sleep, follows a girl sent half a mile to the grocer for sugar, coffee, and bread, who fails to return in an hour. Other prose covers a prairie-dog, a seal, winter fun, Old Whitey, and a council of buzzards.

Verse offers caterpillars, Puss and her three kittens, Fred and Ned, and a Mother Goose melody with music. Astronomy and drawing lessons continue the teaching. The issue keeps the magazine's mix of mystery, animals, and plain morals for children just learning to read.
44962-early-american-poetry-1610-1820-a-:
Early American Poetry is a list of the verse works of the first two hundred years of America, held in a great New York book house. It was built by Frank, of that house. Its note tells that it holds the titles on its shelves on a set day of the late war years.

It first ran in the house sheet, then was struck anew that same fall. Its first names are in the true rank of the past. A priest of Boston leads, with poems on sundry themes, his own and turned from other tongues. The next name is a chief of the free states to come, with his verse of youth. Each line gives place, press, year, and size, so a student can find the book.
484-poor-and-proud-or-the-fortunes-of-ka:
Oliver Optic, pen name of William Taylor Adams, follows Katy Redburn, a poor but proud girl, in this story for young folks. Katy, eleven and ragged, sells fish, pawns a silver watch, and schemes to pay debts and keep her pride. A mayor, a pawnbroker, and kind strangers cross her path.

Optic stresses good principles, politeness, and grit over luck. Katy's ventures grow from a small stock of goods to real success, yet she stays honest through trials. The book charms as a plain moral tale, where a girl's pluck and good conduct win friends and a fair start.
48516-curiosities-of-science-past-and-pr:
John Timbs wrote Curiosities of Science, Past and Present, a book for old and young. It belongs to his series of things not generally known, familiarly explained. The front matter advertises a sister work on painting by Gullick and Timbs. A photograph of the mouth of the great Rosse telescope at Parsonstown serves as an illustration.

Timbs was a tireless popularizer. He turned the wonders of Victorian science into parlor reading: telescopes, telegraphs, steam, and the strange facts of chemistry and natural history, each in a short, clear notice. His method was the anecdote and the marvel, checked against authority. Books like this one carried science to readers who never opened a treatise, and Timbs wrote dozens of them.
49601-a-history-of-deerpark-in-orange-co:
Peter E Gumaer wrote this history of Deerpark in Orange County, New York, issued by the Minisink Valley Historical Society in 1890. A portrait of the author and a cut of the house where he lived front the book. Gumaer says the first settlers near his home asked him to write down what he knew of their forebears. Some still lived in town, and some had gone to other parts of the land.

He put the facts in print so that children who had grown up knowing nothing of their fathers' lives could learn them. In his youth the old people told tales of former times when they met, and those tales, reaching back over eighty miles of valley, feed this small local record.
49753-travels-through-the-interior-parts:
Travels Through the Interior Parts of North America is a travel narrative by Jonathan Carver, covering the years 1766, 1767, and 1768. The third edition, with an account of the author and a full index, was printed in London in 1781. Copper plates, coloured, illustrate the work. Carver had served as a captain of provincial troops in the late war with France.

The advertisement boasts of the book's sale: two large editions were disposed of in two years. Carver travelled from Boston through the Great Lakes to the upper Mississippi and the plains beyond, among peoples no English book had described. His account of the Dakota and his tales of a great river to the Pacific fired the imagination of two generations. The Travels became the standard English source on the interior of the continent, quoted by poets and planners alike.
50338-huxley-and-education-address-at-th:
Henry Fairfield Osborn gave Huxley and Education at the opening of the college year at Columbia University on September 28, 1910. Osborn held the Da Costa chair in zoology. Charles Scribner's Sons issued the speech that year at New York. A verse by Burroughs heads the talk.

Osborn calls opening day the most hopeful day of the year. No student has yet faced the hard task of grasping the modern world of knowledge, he says. Past faults are forgot and hope is high. Osborn asks how his old master Huxley would speak to such a crowd. He draws on Huxley's talks from the winter of 1879 and 1880 and on his essays of 1874 to 1887. Thirty seven years of study and teaching inform the speech.
56698-the-latter-day-prophet-history-of-:
George Cannon, a leader of the Latter-day Saints, wrote this life of Joseph Smith for young people, The Latter-day Prophet, published at Salt Lake City in 1900. His preface says the book was called forth by the needs of the Sunday schools. His larger life of Smith was used in many schools, but it was not written as a textbook for children, and this small volume can be put into the children's own hands.

Teachers may add material from any source, he allows, but the children have a foundation here. The story runs from Smith's boyhood through the founding of the church, told plainly and with faith. The book served for years as the young reader's life of the prophet.
60086-the-boy-travellers-in-the-russian-:
The Boy Travellers in the Russian Empire, by Thomas W Knox, was printed in New York by Harper and Brothers in 1887. Knox wrote The Boy Travellers in the Far East in five volumes and The Young Nimrods.

The title page promises the adventures of two youths in a journey in European and Asiatic Russia. It adds accounts of a tour across Siberia and voyages on the Amoor, the Volga, and other rivers. A visit to Central Asia and travels among the exiles stand in the plan. A history sketch of the empire from its founding to the present time closes the scope. The Far East volumes took the boys to Japan and China, Siam and Java, Ceylon and India, Egypt and Palestine, and Africa. Young readers get Russia by river and rail with two boy guides.
62764-remarks-upon-the-solar-and-the-lun:
Remarks upon the Solar and the Lunar Years, printed at London in 1751, is George, Earl of Macclesfield's letter on the calendar. He wrote it to Martin Folkes, president of the Royal Society, and it was read to that body on May 10, 1750. The subject is the cycle of nineteen years, commonly called the Golden Number, and the epact.

Macclesfield gives a method for finding the time of Easter as most of Europe then kept it. A great table uses the Golden Numbers to show the Paschal full moons. It runs from the reform of the calendar in 1582 all the way to the year 4199. Find the full moon, and the Sunday next after it is Easter Day.
britannica-1911-requesens-luis-de-zuniga:
Luis de Zuniga y Requesens is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Requesens was a Spanish governor of the Netherlands who died in 1576. He had the ill luck to follow the duke of Alva in that post. He had to govern amid hopeless troubles under King Philip the Second. His early career was that of an official and envoy.

The article tells how he won the king's trust as his agent at Rome in 1563. He served as second in command to Don John of Austria in war and at sea. The king named him viceroy in Milan, a post more often given to a great noble. He reached Brussels in 1573 to lead the Netherlands. An empty treasury and unpaid, mutinous troops met him. He died in 1576, worn out by an impossible task.
doe-osti-3018586-selection-effect-in-dar:
Chiara Coviello, supervised by James Annis at Fermilab, wrote this student manuscript, FERMILAB-TM-2894-STUDENT, for the 2022 summer school. Her subject is a puzzle in the Dark Energy Survey's first-year cluster analysis. That analysis returned a matter density near 0.179, with asymmetric errors of a few hundredths. Other surveys cluster around 0.3. A discrepancy demands either new physics or a systematic explanation. Coviello built a procedure to test one candidate: a selection effect in how clusters enter the catalog.

The manuscript first teaches the background it needs. Sections cover dark energy, the survey's data, and the selection-effect bias. The CosmoSIS inference pipeline carries the calculations. Appendices treat the dark matter problem and cluster systematics such as triaxiality. The covariance of cluster counts is dominated by Poisson noise, which the procedure must respect. This one gives the collaboration a repeatable checklist for deciding whether selection, not cosmology, moved the number.
now-or-never-or-the-adventures-of-bobby-:
Lee and Shepard published this Boston edition of Oliver Optic's Now or Never in 1872. Its preface calls the tale a record of youthful struggles, in the world without and the world within. Bobby Bright's success, it says, is not mere wealth and honors. It is a triumph over the temptations that beset the pilgrim on life's plain.

Worldly prosperity is not the truest victory, the preface argues. The author tried to rest the interest on Bobby's devotion to principles, not on business success. Bobby is a smart boy, perhaps too smart, he admits. Young America, he jokes, is older than his father and knows more than his mother. The tale tests that smartness.
podcast-dannyjones-vdbDbIBI4-Y:
Nuclear physicist Max Zamilov joins Danny Jones to share what he calls new proof of lost ancient tech. Zamilov brings an engineer's eye to old stone and metal finds. He argues the finds show power and tools we no longer grasp.

Zamilov walks through the finds that most strain the standard tale of the past. He uses his grasp of heat, force, and wear to test each claim. Jones asks what find would end the debate for good. Listeners get the lost tech case from a man of hard science. The library files the talk as an archive record.
poor-and-proud-or-the-fortunes-of-katy-r:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William Taylor Adams, wrote Poor and Proud as a story for young folks, dedicating it affectionately to his daughter Alice Marie Adams. His preface introduces a new kind of hero for his Library for Young Folks: after two smart boys. Bobby Bright and Harry West, here is a smart girl, Katy Redburn, whose fortunes must hold the same readers. Adams admits a few grains of the romantic, blaming Munchausen and Sindbad on his boyhood shelf.

Katy's success, he promises, depends on nothing magical: good principles, politeness, determined perseverance, and overcoming the foolish pride that snares the feet. Pride and poverty seem enemies, yet Adams argues a pride of character can live in the humblest station. The novel became one of Optic's best-loved moral tales, proof that his formula of pluck and principle worked as well for girls as for his famous boys.
the-boss-of-the-lazy-y: Charles Alden Seltzer wrote The Boss of the Lazy Y, put out in New York by Grosset and Dunlap with rights held by A. C. McClurg and Company in 1915. J. Allen St. John drew the plates. The first parts bring Calumet Marston home and let Betty meet the heir. Calumet's Guardian, Calumet Plays Betty's Game, and The First Lesson come next. A Page from the Past leads to The Toltec Idol and Responsibility.
the-pearl-box-containing-one-hundred-bea:
A pastor compiled The Pearl Box, a book of stories for young people whose title promises one hundred beautiful stories. A transcriber's note warns that the volume in fact holds many stories, but not one hundred; the title overstates the count. The preface says each story carries a moral for the reader's private, social, and public life.

The first story, The Dying Boy, tells of Bertie, who grew weaker until death neared. Hours before the end he revived and asked to be bathed in the river. His mother sponged him instead, dressed him in his green coat and white collar, and seated him at a table with his books and treasures around him. The tales aim to lead youth along the path of duty.
